questions.q: A hash function returns a different number for the same key each time it is called (for example, it mixes in the current time). What breaks?
questions.explain: A hash function must be deterministic. Randomness is allowed only as a fixed seed chosen once when the table is created, so every call during the table's life agrees.
options: Nothing; it just spreads keys more evenly
You can store a value and never find it again, because the lookup computes a different bucket than the insert did
The table becomes O(n log n)

questions.q: A table has 16 buckets and a key's hash is 3,553,150,151. Which bucket does the key go into?
questions.explain: The modulo maps any hash onto the available buckets. When the table resizes to 32 buckets, the same hash maps to a different bucket, which is why every entry must be rehashed.

questions.q: What is a collision in a hash table?
questions.explain: With more possible keys than buckets, collisions are unavoidable. The table handles them by chaining (a list per bucket) or by probing for another slot.
options: Two entries with the same key
Two different keys that land in the same bucket

questions.q: Why must get compare the full key with === after finding the bucket?
questions.explain: Returning the first entry in the bucket would hand one user's session to another user whose token happens to collide. Equal hashes never mean equal keys.
options: To make the lookup slower on purpose
Other keys can share the bucket; the hash only chooses where to look, it does not prove which entry is yours
Because the hash might be negative
It does not need to; equal buckets mean equal keys

questions.q: A table holds 1,200 entries in 2,048 buckets. What is its load factor, and what does it tell you?
questions.explain: Load factor = entries / buckets. Keeping it under a constant (often 0.75 for chaining) keeps chains short, so lookups stay O(1) on average.
options: 2,048 / 1,200 ≈ 1.71: the number of buckets per entry
1,200 / 2,048 ≈ 0.59: the average chain length, which predicts about 1.3 comparisons per successful lookup
0.59: the fraction of buckets that are empty

questions.q: A hash table never resizes and has 8 buckets. What is the average cost of a lookup after 80,000 inserts?
questions.explain: The O(1) average depends on the load factor staying bounded. Without resizing, the load factor grows with n and the table degrades into eight linked lists.
options: O(1): hash tables are always O(1)
O(n): each chain holds about n / 8 entries, so a lookup scans thousands of them

questions.q: Resizing rehashes every entry, which is O(n). Why is set still called O(1) amortized?
questions.explain: It is the same argument as for push on a growable array: doubling makes the expensive steps geometric, and a geometric sum is bounded by a constant times its largest term.
options: Because resizing happens in the background
The bucket count doubles each time, so resizes are rare enough that their total cost over n inserts is O(n)
Because rehashing is free in JavaScript

questions.q: What is the worst-case time of get in a chained hash table with n entries, and when does it happen?
questions.explain: The average is O(1) only if the hash spreads the keys. If every key collides, the table is one long chain. Attackers try to cause exactly this.
options: O(log n), when the table is half full
O(n), when all keys land in the same bucket

questions.q: Why is "add up the character codes" a poor hash function for voucher codes?
questions.explain: A good hash mixes each character into all bits of the result, so position matters and small changes scatter keys across buckets. FNV-1a does this with an XOR and a multiplication per character.
options: Order is ignored, so every anagram (SAVE20, SAVE02) collides, and sums of short strings cover a small range of numbers

questions.q: A server parses JSON bodies into objects. What protects it against hash flooding?
questions.explain: If attackers can predict collisions, one request with thousands of colliding keys makes every insert O(n). A secret seed makes collisions unpredictable; size limits cap the damage of any single request.
options: The engine's seeded (unpredictable) string hash, plus limits on body size and the number of fields accepted
Converting every key to upper case

questions.q: A support tool stores customers in a plain object keyed by username: customers[username]. A customer signs up with the username "constructor". What happens before they are added?
questions.explain: Plain objects inherit keys such as constructor, toString and __proto__. A Map (or Object.create(null)) has no inherited keys.
options: Nothing unusual: the key is missing until you add it
customers["constructor"] already returns a function inherited from Object.prototype, so "does this customer exist?" checks give the wrong answer
The key is converted to a number

questions.q: What is the effect of stock[7] = 10; stock["7"] = 3; on a plain object?
questions.explain: Objects convert non-symbol keys to strings. A Map keeps 7 and "7" as different keys.
options: Two entries: one for the number 7 and one for the string "7"
One entry: object keys are strings, so both lines write the key "7" and the value ends up 3
A TypeError, because keys must be strings

questions.q: Code stores the last login time per user with lastSeen[user] = time, where user is an object. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Objects become strings when used as object keys. Use lastSeen[user.id], or a Map, which uses the object itself as the key.
options: Every user object becomes the string key "[object Object]", so all users share one entry
The object is copied into the key
It throws, because objects cannot be keys

questions.q: const m = new Map([[{ id: "USR-1" }, "admin"]]); Why does m.get({ id: "USR-1" }) return undefined?
questions.explain: Map compares keys with SameValueZero, which for objects means "the same object in memory". Key by a stable string such as user.id when content should decide equality.
options: Object keys are compared by identity: the object in get is a different object from the one stored, even though it looks the same
Because the value is a string
Because get only works with string keys

questions.q: Which is the best fit for a Map rather than a plain object?
questions.explain: A dictionary whose keys come from data and change often is Map's job. Objects are records: a fixed set of known property names, easy to serialize as JSON.
options: A configuration object loaded from a JSON file
All currently open carts, looked up by cart ID, with carts added and removed all day
The options argument of a function

questions.q: A webhook delivered the same order twice, as two separate objects with identical content. Why does new Set(orders) keep both?
questions.explain: new Map(orders.map((o) => [o.id, o])) keeps one entry per id. A Set dedupes primitives and identical references, not equal-looking objects.
options: Sets compare objects by identity, and these are two different objects; dedupe with a Map keyed by order.id instead
Because the orders have different prototypes
Because sets only work with strings

questions.q: You store orders in a Map keyed by order ID. Which question does the map not make fast?
questions.explain: Hashing scatters keys on purpose, so range questions need a full scan: O(n). A sorted array or a tree keyed by time answers ranges efficiently.
options: "What is the total of order ORD-981?"

questions.q: In the hash map two-sum, why does the loop check seen.has(target - price) before adding the current price?
questions.explain: With the check first, [5000] gives no pair, while [5000, 5000] pairs index 0 with index 1, which is correct.
options: Otherwise a single ₦5,000 item could pair with itself for a ₦10,000 target; checking first only finds earlier, different items
Because Map.set must always be the last line of a loop
To find the pair with the largest prices

questions.q: A Node.js service keeps sessions in a Map and never removes expired ones. What happens over weeks of traffic?
questions.explain: An entry in a Map is reachable, so the garbage collector keeps it. Expiry times, periodic cleanup or a bounded LRU cache prevent the leak.
options: The map grows without limit until the process runs out of memory; every store needs expiry or a size limit
The garbage collector removes old entries

questions.q: The lesson's delete moves the last entry of the chain into the removed entry's place and pops. Why is that allowed?
questions.explain: When order is irrelevant, swap-and-pop is O(1) instead of the O(chain length) shifting of splice.
options: The order of entries inside a chain does not matter, so filling the gap with the last entry keeps every entry and avoids shifting
Because chains never contain more than one entry
It is a bug; it loses an entry

questions.q: A price table uses naira amounts like 0.3 as Map keys. Why is prices.get(0.1 + 0.2) undefined?
questions.explain: Floating-point arithmetic is not exact, and a hash table needs exact equality. Integer minor units (kobo) avoid the problem.
options: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, a different number from 0.3; use integer kobo as keys
Because number keys are converted to strings

questions.q: In an open-addressing (linear probing) table, why can delete not simply set the slot back to empty?
questions.explain: Probing searches until it finds the key or an empty slot. Real implementations leave a "deleted" marker (a tombstone) so searches continue past it.
options: Because empty slots cannot be reused
A key stored further along the probe sequence would become unreachable: lookups stop at the first empty slot
Because it would change the hash function
It can; there is no problem

questions.q: An app runs on three server processes behind a load balancer and keeps sessions in a Map in each process. What is the symptom?
questions.explain: Each process has its own memory. A shared store (such as Redis, a hash table on its own server) or sticky routing is needed so that every process sees every session.
options: Users appear logged out at random: a request that reaches a different process finds no session there
Nothing, as long as the maps use the same hash

questions.explain: On a plain object, __proto__ is a special accessor for the prototype: assigning a number to it is ignored, so no key is created. A Map would store it like any other key.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Objects list integer-like keys first, in ascending numeric order, then other string keys in insertion order. A Map keeps pure insertion order.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Maps iterate in insertion order, whatever the key types. The numbers 10 and 2 stay numbers.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only the very same object finds the entry. A spread copy is a new object, and so is a new literal.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The distinct values are 1, "1", NaN and 0. Sets treat NaN as equal to itself and 0 as equal to -0; a number and a string are different.
questions.code:
const values = new Set([1, "1", 1, NaN, NaN, 0, -0]);
console.log(values.size);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each SKU is one key; ?? 0 starts missing counts at zero. The map keeps the order in which each SKU first appeared.

questions.explain: "A" is 65 and "B" is 66, so "AB" and "BA" both sum to 131, and 131 % 4 is 3. "AC" sums to 132, which is 0 modulo 4. Anagrams always collide under this hash.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Setting an existing key replaces its value but keeps its original position. So the key ORD-1 stays first, holding the last object written for it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: At index 2 (₦7,000) the complement ₦3,000 was seen at index 0, so that pair is returned first. A single ₦5,000 item never pairs with itself because the check happens before it is added.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The intersection holds what is in both sets; the difference holds what is in the promo set but not sold. Each operation is O(size) because every membership test is O(1).

questions.q: Build a Map from SKU to product once, then compute the cart total in kobo in O(n + m). Unknown SKUs count as 0.
questions.explain: Indexing the catalogue is O(n); each cart line is then an O(1) lookup instead of an O(n) find. 2 × 240,000 + 3 × 30,000 = 570,000 kobo.

questions.q: Count how many times each SKU was sold and print the best seller and its count, like OIL 3. Use a Map.
questions.explain: One pass to count, one pass over the distinct SKUs to pick the maximum: O(n). Sorting the entries would also work, at O(k log k) for k distinct SKUs.

questions.q: A newsletter list has duplicate emails in different cases and with spaces. Return the list without duplicates, keeping the first spelling of each and ignoring case and surrounding spaces when comparing.
questions.explain: Hash the normalized key, keep the original value. O(n) time and O(n) space. new Set(emails) alone would miss every case and spacing difference.

questions.q: Write pairForCard(prices, target) in O(n) with a Map: return the indexes [i, j] (with i < j) of two different products that sum exactly to the target, or null.
questions.explain: For each price, ask whether its complement appeared earlier. Checking before adding stops an item pairing with itself.

questions.q: Group orders by status into a Map from status to a list of order IDs, and print each group as status: id id in the order statuses first appear.
questions.explain: One pass, O(1) average per lookup: O(n). Map.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.status) does the same grouping in one call (it keeps whole orders rather than IDs).
questions.expected:
paid: ORD-1 ORD-3
pending: ORD-2 ORD-5
refunded: ORD-4

questions.q: Find the first product code in a scan log that appears exactly once. Use two passes over the log and a Map of counts. Print null if there is none.
questions.explain: The first pass counts, the second pass finds the earliest code with a count of 1. Two O(n) passes are still O(n); calling indexOf and lastIndexOf for every code would be O(n²).

questions.q: Print the SKUs in the catalogue that were never sold, in catalogue order, in O(n + m).
questions.explain: Building the set is O(m) and each check is O(1). new Set(catalogue).difference(soldSet) gives the same items as a set.

questions.q: Finish this tiny chained hash table: set must replace the value of an existing key or push a new [key, value] entry into the key's bucket, and get must scan only the key's bucket.
questions.explain: set returns this so calls can be chained, like Map.prototype.set. The full-key comparison in both methods is what makes collisions harmless.
